subject: Filling a matrix from an vector plus indices

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Filling a matrix from an vector plus indices
parts:
Hi folks,

I want to fill a matrix X from a vector Y, and I have a matrix of indices Z relating what element from Y goes where in X. Is there anything faster than the following?

  data{
    matrix[N,N] Z ;
    vector[N] Y ;
  }
  transformed data{
    matrix[N,N] X ;
    for(i in 1:N){
      for(j in 1:N){
        X[i,j] = Y[Z[i,j]] ;
      }
    }
  }    

I was hoping that there might be something like "X = Y[Z]" (and that it was faster than looping), but I guess it's not possible to index with a matrix. Any suggestions?

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

messages.author: cab04b8f0759c712
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Filling a matrix from an vector plus indices
parts:
Hi Mike,

If it's transformed data, then there's nothing faster than looping. I believe you could write up the separate row and col indexes as int array, both the same length, and write something like "X = Y[Z_row, Z_col]" but this will not be any faster than the loop.

I think something you may be mistaking is that vectorization = faster. It's not in general. It's definitely less error prone in this case, but what would be better is to just pass X in properly. If you're looking at a sparse representation, you may want to look at the compressed matrix representation that Krzysztof implemented in the language.


Daniel

Ah, my bad for over-simplifying the situation. While the example I provided filled the second matrix in the transformed data section, in my models I'd actually be building the second matrix in the transformed parameters block. 

I'm actually looking to speed up computation of the covariance matrix in a Gaussian Process by computing only the unique entries (there's usually lots of redundancy in these matrices) then populating the matrix by reference to the unique entries. Here's a gist containing an example of fitting a standard GP versus this faster approach: https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/2e3988449f1790873223cd4e7a499e3f

With the covariance matrix filled with a loop it's about 30% faster than the standard GP (at least, for the scenario of maximum redundancy in the covariance matrix, which occurs when the observations occur on a grid). I was hoping there might be a trick to push it even further, but presumably your prior conclusion (that the loop is as fast as this gets) persists, correct?

This is the general challenge with sparse storage/computation — there’s
an overhead for filling in the matrix randomly instead of sequentially and
you have to enough enough sparsity/redundancy before the speed up
overcomes that overhead.  

The only potential intermediate scenario is if you had a very structured
matrix in which case you would have to exploit the particular structure
to build up the full matrix, for example with low-rank approximations.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Filling a matrix from an vector plus indices
parts:
> On Dec 21, 2016, at 4:01 PM, Mike Lawrence <mike....@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> Ah, my bad for over-simplifying the situation. While the example I provided filled the second matrix in the transformed data section, in my models I'd actually be building the second matrix in the transformed parameters block.
>
> I'm actually looking to speed up computation of the covariance matrix in a Gaussian Process by computing only the unique entries (there's usually lots of redundancy in these matrices) then populating the matrix by reference to the unique entries.

If these are parameters, copying is OK, but you don't want to recreate
them.

So if you've done this:

alpha[1] = beta * gamma;

then you don't want to do this:

alpha[2] = beta * gamma; // BAD --- high overhead

It'll allocate memory in our arena, call constructors, copy
pointers, do arithmetic, and that's just going forward; it'll
also cause extra virtual function calls during and more arithmetic
during derivative calculation.

Instead, you just want to reuse the old entry

alpha[2] = alpha[1]; // GOOD

This just copies a pointer and doesn't add new elements to
the expression graph. And it automatically carries out a kind
of dynamic programming during derivative calculations.

> Here's a gist containing an example of fitting a standard GP versus this faster approach: https://gist.github.com/mike-lawrence/2e3988449f1790873223cd4e7a499e3f
>
> With the covariance matrix filled with a loop it's about 30% faster than the standard GP (at least, for the scenario of maximum redundancy in the covariance matrix, which occurs when the observations occur on a grid). I was hoping there might be a trick to push it even further, but presumably your prior conclusion (that the loop is as fast as this gets) persists, correct?

Yes, loops are fast in Stan. Computation time is
proportional to the size of the expression graph and
the form of functions in it (lgamma is more expensive
than exp is more expensive than multiplication). All
the copying and everything else isn't even usually
measurable. Loops are just compiled to C++ and most
of the vectorization, like in arrays, is just for convenience.

- Bob
